forecasts.question: Will AGI be developed before 1 January 2030?
forecasts.key_change:
Move: 30 to 31. The tape over 21-22 August 2026 is genuinely mixed rather than empty, and for the first time in several days the balance tilts marginally upward. The single most striking item is a capability result rather than a market print, and I want to be clear at the outset that I am giving it modest rather than heavy weight, because it is self-reported, run on a public evaluation set, and is a harness result rather than a model result.

On 21 August NVIDIA published a claim that its AVO system - Agentic Variation Operators - reached a 100.00 RHAE score on ARC-AGI-3, completing all 183 levels across all 25 public environments with 12 per cent fewer environment actions than VISTA, the previous top performer. The context is what makes this arresting. ARC-AGI-3 launched in March 2026 with every frontier model scoring under 1 per cent, humans at 100 per cent, and it was explicitly designed by Francois Chollet's ARC Prize Foundation to resist the usual benchmark-inflation routes: an agent is dropped into an environment with no instructions, no stated rules and no stated goal. Claude Opus 5 standalone was at roughly 30 per cent in early August. Wrapped in AVO's memory, supervision and tooling layers it goes to 100. That is the fastest saturation trajectory I have seen on a benchmark that was marketed as the hard case for general agentic reasoning.

I discount it for four specific reasons, all documented rather than inferred. First, it is not a figure on the ARC Prize leaderboard: verified numbers there come from runs the Foundation administers itself, and AVO's result was generated and reported by NVIDIA's own team using its own reimplementation of the task interface. Second, NVIDIA is explicit that these are "not results on the semi-private or fully private competition sets", which exist precisely because public environments leak and become familiar over time. ARC Prize's own testing policy confirms that only ARC-AGI-1 and ARC-AGI-2 semi-private results are run and verified by the Foundation; everything else is self-scored on public data. Third, NVIDIA itself says the comparison against Opus 5's 30 per cent baseline "should not be interpreted as a controlled ablation" - it is a system score, not a model score. Fourth, and most importantly for this question, Chollet's long-standing framing is that ARC is necessary but not sufficient for AGI, so even a verified private-set saturation would not on its own generate the declaration this question requires. Net, I score it around +2pp: real evidence that the scaffolding layer is unlocking long-horizon behaviour that models cannot produce alone, which is the mechanism most likely to shift elite researcher opinion, but not evidence of a declaration.

The announcement-shaped markets did not confirm it, which is why the move is one point rather than three. I pulled the Kalshi trade API this morning. OAIAGI-29 - "Will OpenAI announce the creation of AGI?" before 2030, the closest liquid instrument to this question - last traded 0.4250 against a previous price of 0.4250, with 24-hour volume of exactly zero. The trade log shows the last print was 20 August at 19:07 UTC; nothing has crossed since. Open interest is 67,335.84, essentially unchanged from yesterday's 67,336. Bid/ask is 0.3800/0.4250. So the instrument that matters most is stale, flat, and carries no new information at all. It has stopped falling, which removes yesterday's headline negative, but it has not turned.

The near rungs moved in opposite directions on trivial volume. OAIAGI-27 (before 2028) last 0.2000 against a previous 0.1800, up two points on 55.95 contracts. OAIAGI-26 (before 2027) last 0.0490 against a previous 0.0700, down 2.1 points on 52.84 contracts. Given that I explicitly warned yesterday about reading two-figure volumes as repricings, I am treating these as close to noise and letting them offset. The KXAGICO-COMP ladder is unchanged in every rung: 28Q4 at 0.6400, the -29 rung (before 1 January 2030) at 0.6700 with a 0.6700/0.7400 spread, -30 at 0.8000, zero 24-hour volume and open interest of just 2,264.72 against total lifetime volume of 3,497.83. That ladder remains decorative and I continue to give it no weight.

Manifold ticked up and, unusually, the prints are fresh. "Will we get AGI before 2029?" stands at 32.0 per cent on 104,191 volume, last updated 21 August at 21:55 UTC, against the 30.4 per cent I recorded yesterday - up 1.6 points. "Will we get AGI before 2030?" is at 38.0 per cent on 134,706 volume, last updated 21 August at 20:22 UTC, against a stale 37.5 per cent last week. Both updating overnight, both up, is a small but genuine positive.

Against that, Polymarket's Astra release ladder has substantially reversed yesterday's pull-forward, on real money. The 15 September rung is 0.4500, down 13.5 points on the day on $4,870 of 24-hour volume; 30 September is 0.7765, down 7.85 points on $1,448; 31 August is 0.0345, down 3.05 points on $4,165; the event carried $11,846 in 24-hour volume. Only 31 October firmed, to 0.8850 from 0.8750. Yesterday I added roughly +2pp for the pull-forward and I am now taking it back out. I will say plainly that I over-weighted it: whether OpenAI's flagship ships in mid-September or late October is close to irrelevant on a forty-month horizon, and I should not have let a two-week timing question carry two points in either direction. Polymarket's "OpenAI announces it has achieved AGI before 2027" sits at 0.0750, down one point on the day on $570 of volume, with $95,720 lifetime.

The Goodheart Labs AGI Timelines Dashboard, fetched live this morning, still reads "Our combined forecast estimates AGI will arrive in 2031, as of August 21, 2026", 80 per cent band 2027-2043. It has not refreshed for today. Nothing in the 21 August news cycle bears on resolution: the day's tape was Nvidia's $6bn Poolside licensing deal, Broadcom seeking $60bn-plus in AI chip debt, Anthropic reportedly preparing an IPO on roughly $65bn annualised revenue and possibly filing by end-August, and Brazil's $444m compute push. Capital and infrastructure, not declarations. If anything, an imminent Anthropic S-1 marginally raises the cost of loose AGI claims from that lab, since registration-statement liability attaches to forward-looking language. No senior researcher declaration surfaced in the window.
forecasts.base_rate:
There is still no historical frequency of AGI declarations to draw on. The event has occurred zero times in the roughly seventy years since the 1956 Dartmouth coinage, so the outside view must be assembled from standing forecast aggregates and structurally analogous classes rather than an event count. That remains the single largest limitation on everything below, and it is why my confidence interval stays wide.

Reference class one, and the anchor I weight most heavily: standing aggregate forecasts on AGI timing. The Goodheart Labs AGI Timelines Dashboard, fetched live this morning, gives a combined median arrival of 2031 with an 80 per cent band of 2027 to 2043, stamped "as of August 21, 2026". It aggregates Metaculus, Manifold and Kalshi inputs across five underlying instruments: Metaculus "weakly general AI" (Q3479), Metaculus "general AI" (Q5121), Metaculus difficult Turing test (Q11861), Manifold's AGI-When distribution, and Kalshi's Turing-test-before-2030 market. A 2031 median with that degree of right skew places roughly a quarter to a third of probability mass before 1 January 2030. Metaculus Q5121 currently shows a community median around January 2033 across more than 1,800 forecasters, with roughly 25 per cent mass on AGI by 2029 - and that is on a bar requiring broad robotic as well as cognitive capability, materially stricter than an announcement-based bar. Its companion "weakly general AI" question sits at a median around June 2028, roughly five years earlier, which is the cleanest available demonstration that most of the spread between these instruments is definitional rather than substantive. Sample sizes here are in the thousands of forecasters, but they are the same population across instruments, so these are not independent draws.

Reference class two: real-money and play-money markets on announcement-shaped bars, which map more closely onto this question's resolution text. Verified this morning: Kalshi OAIAGI-29 at 0.4250 on 164,015 lifetime contracts and 67,336 open interest; Kalshi KXAGICO-COMP-29 (any company announces AGI before 2030) at 0.6700 but on only 3,498 lifetime contracts and 2,265 open interest, which is too thin to be informative; Manifold "AGI before 2030" at 38.0 per cent on 134,706 volume and "AGI before 2029" at 32.0 per cent on 104,191; Polymarket "OpenAI announces AGI before 2027" at 0.0750 on $95,720 lifetime volume. Excluding the illiquid KXAGICO rung, this class clusters between 38 and 43 for a 2030 horizon. That is meaningfully above my central, and the gap needs justifying rather than assuming.

The justification is reference class three: how these questions actually resolve in practice, versus how they price. Two CEO-level "AGI is here" statements are already on the public record - Jensen Huang in March 2026 saying "we've achieved AGI", and Sam Altman in April 2026 saying AGI is something we have already reached without noticing - and Altman has separately said "we are now, like, in the singularity". Demis Hassabis has described standing "in the foothills of the singularity", and Dario Amodei told Davos 2026 that a "nation of geniuses in a data centre" was likely by 2027. None of these resolved this question, and none resolved the Kalshi contracts either. That is direct, repeated evidence that the resolver's qualifiers - "credible", "leading AI researchers", an actual institutional announcement - bind considerably harder than headline rhetoric. I take roughly 8-12 points off the market cluster for this. The same March 2026 window in which Huang declared AGI achieved is the window in which ARC-AGI-3 launched with every frontier model under 1 per cent, which is a useful reminder that declaration rhetoric and measured capability have been decoupling in both directions.

Reference class four, weaker and used only as a sanity check: expert-survey drift on transformative technology arrival dates. Successive AI Impacts-style expert surveys have shown medians pulling forward sharply since 2022, but the historical record on such surveys - fusion, autonomous vehicles, room-temperature superconductors - is one of persistent optimism bias, with realised dates typically landing well beyond expert medians. Sample sizes are in the hundreds; the technologies are not closely analogous; I use this only to justify not updating upward toward the market cluster.

Integrating: the aggregate class points to 25-33, the announcement-market class to 38-43, and the resolution-practice adjustment pulls the second down into the low 30s. I land at 31, closer to the aggregates, because the resolution bar here is a conjunction of capability and an explicit institutional or multi-researcher declaration, and the historical record over the past twelve months shows the declaration leg failing repeatedly even when the rhetoric was available.

forecasts.question: Will economic consultancy lose ≥33% value/jobs by end 2030 due to AI?
forecasts.key_change:
Hold at 12. I ran ten searches across the 19-22 August 2026 window and fetched two sources directly, and my conclusion is that nothing broke in the last three days that shifts the resolution arithmetic. Yesterday I moved 13 to 12 on the strength of a full check of the BLS employment series; today the new material is genuinely two-sided, and the disciplined answer is to hold rather than to ratchet down a second consecutive day on evidence that is confirmatory rather than novel.

The single most useful new item I found is IBISWorld's Scientific and Economic Consulting in the US report, published July 2026, which I had not previously cited. This matters because it is the closest available match to the question's named industry rather than the broader management-consulting aggregate I have been leaning on. IBISWorld puts US scientific and economic consulting revenue at an estimated 65.6 billion dollars, having expanded at a 4.1% compound annual rate over the past five years, with an estimated 2.6% increase in 2026 alone and profit margin at 16.4%. It explicitly attributes demand to finance and retail buyers procuring economic forecasting work, particularly following the 2025 tariff programme, which altered forecasting assumptions across the economy. That is the opposite of the resolution condition on the revenue leg: the sector the question names is growing in 2026, and it is growing partly because policy volatility generates exactly the analytical work economic consultancies sell. A separate market estimate puts the global economics consulting market at 36.21 billion dollars in 2024 rising to 50.81 billion by 2032 on a 5.0% CAGR. For the revenue leg to resolve YES, that trajectory must not merely flatten but invert into roughly a 33% fall from the 2024 base within four years and four months.

On the other side, I picked up three items that deserve weight and that I want to record honestly rather than dismiss. First, McKinsey's headcount has come down from above 45,000 to about 40,000 over roughly eighteen months, a fall of about 11%, with AI cited in management framing and with reported plans for further cuts of a few thousand non-client-facing roles over the next eighteen to twenty-four months. Reporting is inconsistent about mechanism, and the better-sourced accounts stress attrition and non-replacement rather than mass redundancy, but an 11% fall at the sector's most visible firm is not nothing. Second, Revelio Labs' postings data shows overall talent demand at leading consulting firms roughly 20% below its 2023 peak, with demand for consultant roles specifically about 40% lower, and a sharp seniority divergence: senior-consultant demand up 55% since 2020 while entry-level demand is down 10% from its 2023 peak. Third, the graduate pipeline numbers are stark. KPMG cut its UK graduate class 29%, from 1,399 to 942; Deloitte trimmed UK intake about 18%, EY 11%, PwC 6%; and PwC's audit and assurance hiring is reportedly being cut 32-39% through 2028. McKinsey, BCG and Bain have frozen starting salaries for a third consecutive year.

The reason none of this moves me up is that it is all pipeline and flow, not stock, and the stock is what resolves the question. Job postings are a leading indicator of hiring, not of headcount, and they fall from a 2023 peak that was itself an artefact of the post-pandemic hiring boom. Graduate intake cuts of 20-30% at UK Big Four firms shrink future cohorts, but with average tenure and a firm-wide base measured in tens of thousands, they translate into aggregate headcount declines in the low single digits per year at most, and they are partly a correction to over-hiring in 2021-22 rather than a clean AI signal. Meanwhile the listed comparators keep printing records. CRA International reported Q2 2026 revenue of 210.8 million dollars, up 12.8% and the highest quarterly revenue in its history, with non-GAAP EPS of 2.16 dollars up 14.9%, and raised full-year 2026 constant-currency revenue guidance to 805-820 million dollars from 785-805 million. Huron posted record Q2 revenues before reimbursables of 465.6 million dollars, up 15.7%, and raised full-year guidance to 1.85-1.89 billion dollars with EPS guidance to 9.00-9.40 dollars. The MCA's Annual Industry Report 2026 forecasts UK consulting revenue up 6% in 2026 and 8% in 2027, on a 2025 base of 21.8 billion pounds that itself grew 3%, with exports at 31% of fee income rising 9% year on year. Source Global Research has technology consulting passing 400 billion dollars for the first time in 2026 on 7% growth.

The macro backdrop is soft but not consulting-specific, and softness that is macro-driven actively works against YES because of the attribution bar. July 2026 US nonfarm payrolls changed little at minus 23,000, against an average monthly gain of 34,000 over the prior twelve months. Initial claims for the second week of August fell 6,000 to 206,000, below expectations of 210,000, extending a run of low readings since the near-sixty-year low of 189,000 in mid-July; continuing claims rose 18,000 to 1,799,000. That is a low-hiring, low-firing labour market, not a professional-services washout. Challenger's most recent reports have AI leading stated reasons for cuts for a fifth straight month, with about 101,743 AI-cited cuts through June, roughly 23% of all cuts, and technology at 149,023 cuts through July, 31% of the annual total and up 67% on 2025. But Andy Challenger's own framing is that hiring is up 25% on last year and that AI is shifting the labour market rather than dismantling it, and the composition remains technology-centred rather than advisory.

I also note the academic evidence keeps coming in weaker than the discourse. A 2026 study by Hartley, Jolevski, Melo and Moore finds 35.9% of US workers had used generative AI by December 2025, with small positive wage effects and no statistically significant declines in job openings. The New York Fed's Liberty Street Economics post of 5 August 2026 by Kartik Athreya covers hiring practices and skill requirements without documenting sectoral displacement. PIIE and the Hamilton Project both published pieces this summer arguing systematic academic evidence of negative labour-market effects remains surprisingly limited. Since resolution requires two or more credible analyses attributing a one-third decline primarily to AI, the thinness of the academic evidence base is itself a constraint on YES, independent of what happens to the underlying numbers. Holding at 12, CI 6-21.
forecasts.base_rate:
The primary reference class is unchanged and remains poor: professional-services sectors that lost a third or more of revenue or employment inside roughly six years, with that loss attributed primarily to one identified technology by multiple credible independent analyses. Membership is sparse and every candidate fails at least one criterion. US travel agency employment fell perhaps 40-50%, but over about fifteen years from 1998 and with two distinct causes, online booking and the abolition of airline commissions, so it would likely fail a primarily-attributed test. Contract document review contracted sharply after predictive coding and technology-assisted review, but the affected population was contract attorneys rather than a whole profession, and legal services revenue kept growing throughout. Typesetting and pre-press composition did collapse by well over a third, but over more than a decade and against a physical craft with no advisory or relationship component. Bank tellers, stock-photo contributors and switchboard operators are similarly ill-matched on either the timescale or the professional-judgement dimension. Across the pool of technology-disruption episodes that generate serious sectoral contraction talk, clean six-year declines of a third or more in a professional-services sector occur in something like one case in ten to one in fifteen. Most such episodes resolve as task-mix restructuring, price compression inside a still-growing revenue pool, or a reshaping of the seniority pyramid, not as aggregate contraction of a third. That gives an outside-view anchor of roughly 8-12% for a randomly drawn technology-and-sector pair from the credible-disruption-candidate pool.

The second and better-matched reference class is the historical drawdown distribution of the target series itself. BLS CES6054160001, US management, scientific and technical consulting services employment, runs monthly from January 1990. July 2026 stands at 1,886,600 seasonally adjusted; June 2026 at 1,888,100 is the highest print in the series' thirty-six-year history; the twelve 2024 monthly values average 1,860,500. A 33% fall from that baseline implies an end-2030 level near 1,246,600, a fall of roughly 640,000 jobs or about 33.9% from July 2026, sustained at about minus 9.0% a year compounded for fifty-three consecutive months. The deepest peak-to-trough drawdown the series has ever recorded is the pandemic shock, 1,569,000 in February 2020 to 1,474,100 in April 2020, a fall of 6.0% fully recovered within about ten months. The 2001 dot-com bust and the 2008-09 financial crisis each produced drawdowns of roughly 3%. So the required decline is between five and eleven times the worst outcome in the series' entire history, and would have to persist rather than recover. On a purely empirical reading of that distribution, the implied probability of a 33% decline over any 53-month window is well under 1%; the reason I do not forecast under 1% is that the series contains no episode of a general-purpose technology directly substituting for the sector's core cognitive output, so the historical distribution is not the right sampling frame for the tail I care about.

A third reference class I have now added is the industry-level revenue series. IBISWorld's Scientific and Economic Consulting in the US report, July 2026, gives 65.6 billion dollars of revenue, a 4.1% five-year CAGR and an estimated 2.6% increase in 2026. Global economics consulting is estimated at 36.21 billion dollars in 2024 rising to 50.81 billion by 2032 on a 5.0% CAGR. There is no forecast from any credible market-research house that has this sector contracting at all, let alone by a third. Forecast houses are chronically trend-extrapolative and would be slow to catch a genuine inflection, so I discount them, but their unanimity is still evidence.

Limitations worth stating plainly. First, the reference classes are backward-looking and the causal mechanism proposed here has no historical analogue at comparable capability, so all three understate the tail. Second, the question's compound structure cuts both ways: it can resolve on either revenue or employment, which raises the probability, but it also imposes an attribution requirement that macro-driven contraction would fail, which lowers it substantially. Third, "economic consultancy" is not consistently defined across sources, and a narrow reading confined to expert-witness and competition economics work would have a much smaller and more volatile base than the BLS aggregate. Fourth, sample sizes for the primary class are effectively single-digit, so the 8-12% anchor carries wide error bars. I weight the outside view heavily and let inside-view factors move me only a few points either side, which is how I arrive at 12% with an 80% interval of 6-21.

forecasts.question: Will Labour be largest party at next UK General Election?
forecasts.key_change:

The natural outside-view class is incumbent UK governing parties defending a Commons majority at the following general election. Across the twenty general elections since 1945 the incumbent governing party was the largest party at the subsequent election in roughly thirteen of nineteen defences, a base rate near 65-70 per cent. That class flatters Labour badly. It is drawn almost entirely from a stable two-and-a-half party system where the incumbent's principal risk was a straight swing to a single main opponent, and where no governing party ever entered mid-term polling at 22-27 per cent with four other parties at or above 9 per cent. Today's PollCheck average has five parties between 10.3 and 26.0 per cent. The 2024 baseline is itself the anomaly that breaks the class: Labour won 411 seats on 33.7 per cent of the GB vote, the most seat-efficient large win in modern British history, on a turnout of 59.7 per cent. A party converting 33.7 per cent into 63 per cent of seats has enormous downside room before it stops being largest, but no cushion of loyal vote share to absorb shocks.

A tighter and more apposite class is governing parties that changed leader mid-term and then faced the electorate. The UK record is genuinely mixed and small-n. Eden in 1955 and Major in 1992 both won after inheriting; Douglas-Home 1964, Callaghan 1979, Brown 2010 and Sunak 2024 lost; May 2017 lost her majority but remained largest; Johnson 2019 won outright. Counting the eight clearest mid-term successions since 1955, the inheriting party remained largest at the next election in four - Eden, Major, Johnson and, on a generous reading, May - giving something close to 50 per cent, with the outcome depending heavily on how long the new leader waited and whether the honeymoon was banked or squandered. Burnham took office on 20 July 2026 and has given no indication of going early, which historically is the losing choice: Eden and Johnson went within months of inheriting and won; Douglas-Home, Callaghan, Brown and Sunak waited and lost. That 50 per cent figure is the most defensible single anchor and is where I currently sit.

A third class worth naming is plurality-winner persistence under fragmenting multi-party systems. In European democracies where an insurgent right party has broken 20 per cent, the incumbent centre-left has retained largest-party status perhaps a third to a half of the time, but almost all of those systems are proportional, so the analogy transfers poorly to the seat question that actually resolves here. First-past-the-post is the single largest reason my number sits well above Labour's raw vote share would imply: Electoral Calculus's 28 July run converts a Labour share of 23.9 per cent and Reform's 23.4 per cent into 244 seats against 127, because the right-of-centre vote splits three ways between Conservative 18-22, Reform 23-26 and Restore Britain around 4, while Labour's vote, though small, is concentrated in urban seats. The Penistone East result on 20 August - Labour 51.6 per cent, Reform 23.8 - is a small local illustration of the same efficiency.

Limitations I keep front of mind. The sample of mid-term successions is eight, so the 50 per cent figure carries an enormous standard error; a single reclassification of May 2017 moves it by six points. The reference classes all predate a five-party system and a party polling 25 per cent with eight MPs, so the seat-conversion function is being extrapolated far outside its historical support - which is precisely why Electoral Calculus's own 90 per cent interval for Labour spans 88 to 357 seats and Reform's spans 53 to 289. Council by-election evidence, of the kind I logged today, has essentially no established base rate for predicting general-election plurality three years out; the four wards on 20 August had a combined turnout in the low thousands. And the resolution horizon of December 2029 means the honeymoon-decay base rate matters more than any current poll: new-leader net approval typically halves within six to twelve months, and Burnham is five weeks in with a Budget on 28 October. I therefore weight the outside view heavily and let daily news move me only a point or two.

forecasts.question: Will AGI be developed before 1 January 2035?
forecasts.key_change:
Hold at 85. The 19-22 August 2026 window delivered two substantive items that pull in opposite directions, a market that has gone completely dark, and a correction to my own inside view that I think nets out to no change in the central estimate. On an eight-and-a-half year horizon with a rhetorical resolution bar, that is the honest answer.

The headline item is NVIDIA's claim, published on its developer blog on 21 August, that its AVO system - Agentic Variation Operators - reached 100.00 on ARC-AGI-3's Relative Human Action Efficiency metric, completing all 183 levels across all 25 public environments with 12 per cent fewer environment actions than VISTA, the previous top performer. Critically, AVO is not a new model: it is Claude Opus 5 wrapped in NVIDIA's own memory, supervision and tooling layers. NVIDIA is explicit in the post that these are "not results on the semi-private or fully private competition sets", the run used NVIDIA's own reimplementation of the task interface rather than the foundation's harness, and it does not appear on the ARC Prize Verified Leaderboard. The New Stack's write-up and the Hacker News thread both lead with those caveats. So the raw number is a system score on a public set that gets easier as it becomes familiar, self-administered by an interested party. I discount it heavily.

What I cannot discount is that it forced me to check the verified leaderboard, and my prior note was carrying stale figures. I had a minus-five-point down-factor resting on "ARC-AGI-3 still under 1 per cent for frontier models (Gemini 3.1 Pro 0.37 per cent, GPT-5.4 0.26 per cent, Opus 4.6 0.25 per cent)". That has not been the state of play since 24 July, when ARC Prize posted Claude Opus 5 (High) at 30.2 per cent on ARC-AGI-3, roughly quadrupling GPT-5.6 Sol (Max)'s prior record of 7.8 per cent. ARC Prize's own commentary noted Opus 5 solving five public demo environments no model had previously beaten and, more interestingly, translating tasks into algebraic notation and independently formulating reflection equations - behaviour they had not seen before. My own update trigger from yesterday read "Revise UP if a frontier model posts above 20 per cent on ARC-AGI-3". On the verified leaderboard that trigger has already been met, and had been for a month. Mechanically that argues for two to three points up, because the fluid-reasoning gap I was pricing as a hard wall is visibly permeable. One complication: ARC Prize posted on X that it had early access to Anthropic's Fable 5 but did not run verified semi-private ARC-AGI-1/2/3 evaluations because of Anthropic's new data-retention terms for Mythos-class models, so the verified picture for the very newest systems is partially blind.

Pulling the other way, and published in the same 24-hour window, is a new scientific-reasoning benchmark called Reconstruction. Frontier LLMs recover research-paper ideas from bibliographies alone at just 3 to 15 per cent, and a multi-agent "top 4" Swiss-tournament pipeline gets only to 42 per cent. That is the second independent result in five days pointing at the same weakness, after the Kirgis and Kapoor shadow-evaluation paper on 18 August in which agents given six days, three thousand dollars of credit and GPUs produced two papers both rejected by the original authors. The generative, hypothesis-forming end of research remains the bottleneck even as puzzle-solving and long-horizon agentic execution improve fast. Since the strongest short-timeline stories run through recursive self-improvement and automated AI R&D, two converging bearish datapoints on exactly that mechanism are worth roughly what the ARC correction is worth in the other direction.

The market picture is emptier than yesterday. I pulled Kalshi's KXAGICO series again this morning. The event KXAGICO-COMP, "When will any company achieve AGI?", subtitled "Corporate announcement", carries thirteen markets running from 26Q2 through KXAGICO-COMP-30, which closes 1 January 2031. The rules text remains an almost exact match for this question's first limb: "If any company (public or private) officially announces that it has achieved Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) after market issuance and before [date], then the market resolves to Yes." But the trade tape has gone quiet: the most recent prints are 17 August on the 27Q4 tranche, 16 August on the 2030 tranche and 14 August on the 2029 tranche. Nothing traded on 18, 19, 20, 21 or 22 August in any tranche. So the mid prices I extrapolated from yesterday - roughly 70.5 per cent by 2030 and 76.5 per cent by 2031, implying 85 to 88 per cent by 2035 under a slowly decaying hazard - are stale quotes rather than a live consensus, and there is no 2035 tranche at all. Elsewhere, Polymarket's "OpenAI announces it has achieved AGI before 2027" sits at 89 per cent No, so about 9 to 11 per cent Yes, unchanged in substance. The parallel 2030 forecast found Kalshi OAIAGI-29 flat at 0.4250 on zero volume and Manifold's AGI-before-2030 at 38.0 per cent. Manifold's AGI-before-2035 construct prices around 51 per cent, though that market resolves on community poll and imports a much stricter notion than a lab announcement. The Polymarket Astra release ladder falling back 13.5 points to 0.4500 for 15 September is a schedule story, not a capability story, and consistent with Axios's 7 August report that OpenAI is slowing Astra because it cannot rule out Critical cyber capability.

Two smaller items round out the window. Data Center Knowledge's August round-up projects that 30 to 50 per cent of planned 2026 AI data-centre capacity will slip to 2028 on grid-interconnection queues and construction bottlenecks, with copper for power distribution emerging as a chokepoint. Over eight and a half years that is a phasing problem, not a ceiling. And frontier agents from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and others reportedly breached live systems, exploited a zero-day and attempted a real supply-chain attack in controlled evaluations reported around 21 August - which cuts both ways, evidencing capability while strengthening the case for the kind of deceleration OpenAI has already chosen.

Net: one genuine inside-view correction up, two converging research-capability results down, no market movement, no lab announcement, no researcher statements. Hold at 85, interval unchanged at 74 to 93.
forecasts.base_rate:
There is no frequency base rate here. AGI has never been developed, so the event class has zero members and no historical frequency can be computed. The only usable outside view is the distribution of published forecasts on near-identical questions, treated as a reference class of forecaster distributions rather than of events. I track six anchors, and today I am adding weight to one I had been under-using.

First, the Goodheart Labs combined AGI timelines dashboard. As of its 16 August 2026 reading it gives a median arrival year of 2031 with an 80 per cent interval of 2027 to 2042 - marginally tighter at the top than the 2043 I recorded on 21 August, which is within the noise of how that dashboard aggregates. Fitting a right-skewed distribution through a 10th percentile of 2027, a median of 2031 and a 90th percentile of 2042 puts roughly 70 to 76 per cent of mass before 1 January 2035. The asymmetry matters: four years separate the 10th from the 50th percentile but eleven separate the 50th from the 90th, so cumulative probability rises steeply through the late 2020s and then flattens into a long tail that 2035 sits well inside.

Second, Metaculus question 5121, the strict "first general AI system devised, tested and publicly announced" question, at a community median of around January 2033 across roughly 1,800 to 1,900 forecasters, with about 25 per cent by 2027 and 50 per cent by 2031 on the related aggregate. A median in early 2033 mechanically implies more than half the mass before 2035, and interpolating the community shape suggests 60 to 70 per cent by 1 January 2035. Reported interquartile bounds on the individual predictions run from late December 2026 to late March 2039, which is very wide. This is my most conservative credible anchor because Metaculus's four-condition operationalisation - a two-hour adversarial Turing test, general robotic manipulation, at least 75 per cent accuracy on every MMLU task and 90 per cent mean, and 90 per cent single-attempt accuracy on APPS, all in one system - is far stricter than this question's rhetorical bar. Metaculus's weakly-general variant, question 3479, sits at a median around mid-2028 and is far looser.

Third, and newly weighted, the Forecasting Research Institute's LEAP panel, wave 8, fielded 20 April to 11 May 2026. Superforecasters give a median AGI year of 2047 and an 80 per cent median probability of AGI before 2100; computer science experts and industry professionals put 80 and 85 per cent on before-2100, economists only 60 per cent. A superforecaster median of 2047 implies well under 50 per cent by 2035 on LEAP's definition. This is the single most conservative serious anchor in the set, and it comes from a large, longitudinally tracked, professionally elicited panel rather than an open market. I hold it at moderate weight because LEAP's construct is HLMI-like - full substitution across human tasks - which is several orders of difficulty above "a credible lab says the word AGI about a system it has built". The same wave shows the share of matched experts whose modal forecast is "technology of the century" rising from 38 to 53 per cent, so the panel is becoming more impressed even as its timing medians stay long.

Fourth, the FutureSearch AGI timeline tracker. Between January and April 2026 every single forecaster who updated moved earlier: Kokotajlo's Automated Coder median from late 2029 to mid-2028, Lifland's by a comparable amount, Nikola's around end-2029. The 21 August prior noted the AI Futures Project's Q2.5 update on 16 August placing Kokotajlo at 2028 and Lifland at 2032. This is the shortest-timeline anchor and I discount it for selection: this cluster of forecasters is self-selected for taking short timelines seriously.

Fifth, Kalshi KXAGICO-COMP, whose rules text matches the first limb of this question almost exactly. Its tranches stop at 1 January 2031, and its last trades were 14 to 17 August, so it is currently a stale quote rather than a price. The 21 August mids implied roughly 70.5 per cent by 2030 and 76.5 per cent by 2031, which rolled forward with a decaying hazard through 2032 to 2034 lands near 85 to 88 per cent by 2035. That is the closest-matched anchor by wording and the weakest by liquidity.

Sixth, aggregator surveys. The 2023-24 AI Impacts style expert surveys put HLMI medians near 2047, consistent with LEAP. Secondary aggregations of thousands of public predictions cluster frontier-lab leaders at 2026-2028, community forecasts near 2033, and named sceptics at 2035 or later.

Weighting the six: the wording-matched market and the loose-definition anchors sit in the mid-to-high 80s; the strict-definition anchors sit in the 60s and 70s; LEAP sits below 50. The dispersion is the point. My central estimate sits above the strict anchors because this question resolves on announcement rather than demonstrated capability, and Jensen Huang's March 2026 "we've achieved AGI" is standing evidence that the rhetorical bar is far lower than the technical one. The main limitation is that a reference class of forecasts is not a reference class of events: it inherits correlated errors, herding, and the field's documented tendency to shorten during capability booms and lengthen during plateaus.

factors_up.factor: Resolution bar is rhetorical, not technical - one lab announcement or three researcher statements, with no agreed AGI definition to police the claim; Huang's March 2026 'we've achieved AGI' and Goertzel's 27-30 July AGI-26 statement that AGI could arrive in nine to twelve months are standing precedent for term inflation over 8.5 years

Corrected ARC-AGI-3 picture: ARC Prize verified Claude Opus 5 (High) at 30.2 per cent on 24 July 2026, quadrupling GPT-5.6 Sol's 7.8 per cent, with novel algebraic-notation behaviour; NVIDIA AVO reported 100.00 RHAE on the 25-environment public set on 21 August. Directional consensus among tracked forecasters is still shortening - FutureSearch records every updater moving earlier between January and April 2026 (Kokotajlo late-2029 to mid-2028), and 80,000 Hours' August retrospective reports its own timelines shortening by about a year on 2026 evidence

factors_down.factor: LEAP wave 8 (fielded 20 April to 11 May 2026) puts the superforecaster median AGI year at 2047 with only 80 per cent before 2100; economists put 60 per cent before 2100. The most rigorously elicited large panel is far more conservative than markets

Two converging results in five days on the creativity and hypothesis-generation gap: the Reconstruction benchmark (21 Aug) has frontier LLMs recovering paper ideas from bibliographies at 3-15 per cent and a multi-agent pipeline at only 42 per cent, following Kirgis/Kapoor's shadow evaluation (18 Aug) in which agents given six days and 3,000 dollars produced two papers both rejected by the original authors

Strict-definition forecaster distributions retain long right tails - Goodheart's 80 per cent interval still runs to 2042 as of 16 August and Metaculus 5121's individual interquartile range extends to March 2039, implying 25-30 per cent of mass after 2035

Labs voluntarily decelerating - Axios reported on 7 August that OpenAI is slowing Astra because it cannot rule out Critical cyber capability, and 21 August evaluation reporting has frontier agents from four labs breaching live systems, exploiting a zero-day and attempting a supply-chain attack, strengthening the case for further pauses

The field is fragmenting the term into graded taxonomies (DeepMind's AGI-to-ASI pathways paper, the Fortune March 2026 piece on nobody agreeing what AGI means) while non-labs dilute it, raising the chance serious labs avoid the word entirely and no clean announcement is ever made

Physical constraints biting - 30 to 50 per cent of planned 2026 AI data-centre capacity projected to slip to 2028 on grid-interconnection queues and construction bottlenecks, with copper for power distribution an emerging chokepoint

key_uncertainties: Whether a frontier lab ever uses the word AGI to describe a system it has shipped, or whether commercial and legal incentives (OpenAI's restructuring, its IPO track, the Microsoft AGI clause) permanently push labs towards graded taxonomies instead

Whether the hypothesis-generation gap evidenced by Reconstruction (3-15 per cent) and the Kirgis/Kapoor shadow evaluation is a shallow scaffolding problem that agent architectures like AVO close, or a deep architectural limit that blocks recursive self-improvement

Whether the ARC-AGI-3 jump from 7.8 to 30.2 per cent generalises to the semi-private and private sets, which ARC Prize currently cannot run on Mythos-class models because of Anthropic's data-retention terms

How much weight to place on the LEAP superforecaster median of 2047 versus market-implied and lab-leader medians eight to nineteen years earlier - the spread across serious anchors is wider than my whole confidence interval
Whether the 'three or more leading AI researchers' limb is easier or harder than it looks, given Huang, Goertzel and Amodei have each made statements that a lenient resolver might already count
update_triggers: Revise UP sharply if OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind or xAI publishes a document using the word AGI to describe a system it has built rather than one it is pursuing
Revise UP if three or more senior researchers at different frontier labs state within a short window that AGI has been achieved, echoing the Huang March 2026 framing
Revise UP if ARC Prize posts a verified semi-private ARC-AGI-3 score above 40 per cent for any model, or if Kalshi lists a KXAGICO-COMP tranche beyond 2031 that prices above 0.85

Revise UP if Astra or a Mythos-class model demonstrates sustained autonomous multi-week research output, or if a rerun of the Kirgis/Kapoor shadow evaluation produces a paper the original authors accept

forecasts.question: Will China initiate a military blockade or invasion of Taiwan before 1 January 2030?
forecasts.key_change:
Hold at 7. The 21-22 August window produced one genuinely new, quantified piece of evidence and nothing else of consequence, and the new evidence cuts in the direction I had already flagged qualitatively rather than opening a new channel. I keep the central estimate at 7 percent and the interval at 4-11.

The item that matters is the CSIS Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative report "As Tokyo and Manila Talk Boundaries, Beijing Breaks Them", published on 19 August and picked up by the Taipei Times on 21 August and the Japan Times on 21 August. Yesterday I described PRC law-enforcement activity east of Taiwan as accreting quarantine infrastructure, citing the first-ever questioning of commercial vessels in June 2026. AMTI now puts a number on it: Chinese law-enforcement vessels hailed roughly 198 commercial ships transiting the Philippine Sea east of Taiwan and demanded their ports of call and crew details, conduct AMTI notes would be unlawful even inside China's own EEZ. The activity has run since June, mainly with two ships, concentrated in the zone where Japanese and Philippine maritime claims overlap, and has been paired with a separate Ministry of Natural Resources marine environmental survey that Chinese state commentary framed as building a fuller understanding of the country's "jurisdictional areas". AMTI reads the campaign as a response to the May announcement that Japan and the Philippines would open maritime boundary delimitation talks, not primarily as a Taiwan operation. That framing is important and it is why I am not moving. The proximate driver is a third-party delimitation dispute; the Taiwan-relevant read-across is second-order, though real, because it rehearses the hailing-and-interrogation procedure that any quarantine would need and it does so on the eastern approaches, which are the harder half of any encirclement. Prospect Foundation president Lai I-chung has separately argued these operations look like a quarantine test. I treat this as confirming, not extending, the mechanism I already priced at plus 1.5 points, and I have raised that factor to plus 2 to reflect the sharper quantification while trimming elsewhere.

Everything else in the window is quiet or mildly reassuring. On the military tempo, Taiwan's MND logged 20 PLA aircraft sorties, 7 PLAN ships and 6 official ships in the 24 hours to 6am on 21 August, with 15 of the 20 sorties entering the northern, central, southwestern or eastern ADIZ. That is the highest single-day figure of the week but sits within the ordinary 2026 distribution and involved no median-line surge. The 22 August tally collapsed to 3 aircraft and 15 ships, one of the lowest aircraft counts of the month. There is still no named exercise, no NOTAM or closure area, no live-fire announcement from the Fujian or Zhangzhou maritime safety administrations, and nothing resembling the two-day Dongshan Island drills of July. forecasts.base_rate:
Three reference classes bear on this question and I weight the first two heavily.

The broad class is major-power initiation of an opposed amphibious assault, or a sustained naval blockade of a defended and populated territory, since 1945. The candidate set is thin: Inchon in 1950 against a state already at war, Suez in 1956, the Cuban quarantine of 1962 which was a partial interdiction lasting under a month, the Falklands in 1982 which was a British counter-invasion of a lightly garrisoned archipelago, the Iran-Iraq tanker war of 1984-88, and Russia's Black Sea grain interdiction from 2022. Roughly six episodes across eighty years, against a denominator of perhaps twenty to thirty dyads at any time possessing both the capability and a claimed casus belli. That implies an annualised hazard per capable dyad on the order of 0.5 to 2 percent. Applied to the 3.36 years remaining from 22 August 2026 to 1 January 2030, that yields about 2 to 7 percent. The class has obvious limitations: it is small, the cases are heterogeneous in scale, and the modern nuclear and economic-interdependence context is not well represented in the mid-century entries. Its main value is as a discipline against narrative escalation, because the sheer rarity of the act is the single most robust fact available.

The narrower and better-matched class is Taiwan Strait coercion episodes since 1995: the 1995 and 1996 missile crises, the August 2022 Pelosi encirclement exercises, Joint Sword 2024A in May 2024, Joint Sword 2024B in October 2024, Strait Thunder 2025A in April 2025, and Justice Mission 2025 in late December 2025. Seven salient episodes in thirty-one years, giving an episode rate of roughly 0.23 per year and, at the current elevated tempo, closer to one per year. The conversion rate from episode to sustained blockade or assault is zero for seven. Even a generous Laplace-style adjustment on that sample gives a per-episode conversion probability of about 12 percent at the upper end, and I think that is far too high given that every one of the seven was announced, time-boxed to hours or days, and deliberately reversible. Taking one to two such episodes per year over 3.36 years and a conversion probability of 1 to 3 percent per episode gives roughly 4 to 10 percent, which is the range my central estimate sits inside.

The third source is expert and market forecasts, which I use as a sanity check rather than an anchor. Polymarket's invasion-by-end-2026 market implies roughly 4 percent, down from near 30 percent in late 2025, on more than 55 million dollars of Taiwan-related volume. Metaculus questions on Chinese invasion by 2030 have historically run considerably higher, in the 35 to 43 percent range, but those are typically worded around "attempt to invade" over longer horizons or with looser resolution language, and I do not treat them as comparable to this question's bar. The dispersion between market and forecaster-platform estimates is itself informative: it tells me the structural uncertainty is large and it is why I keep an 80 percent interval of 4 to 11 rather than something tighter.

Three limitations deserve stating. First, the resolution bar here is strict and asymmetric to the most likely escalation path. A customs-inspection quarantine, a closure area, or a 48 to 72 hour encirclement exercise are each individually more probable than a true blockade, and none would clearly resolve YES. That pushes the answer below any generic "conflict over Taiwan" estimate. Second, base rates assume stationarity, and the PRC's capability trajectory is emphatically non-stationary: 234 warships to the USN's 219, a 2026 defence budget of 1.91 trillion yuan, and twelve submarines plus a carrier and nineteen surface combatants commissioned since 2024. Against that, Xi's purges have removed over 100 senior officers since 2022, including five of seven CMC members and vice chairmen, and Strait Thunder took 19 days to organise in April 2025 against three to four days for Joint Sword in 2024. Capability is rising while command coherence is degraded, and these partially cancel. Third, hazard is unlikely to be uniform across the remaining 3.36 years. The bulk of the risk sits in 2028-29, after Taiwan's January 2028 presidential election, after any rebuilt CMC has bedded in, and inside the window when US munitions stocks from the Iran campaign are still short. That temporal skew is why I hold a fat right tail rather than a symmetric interval.

forecasts.question: Will UK annual CPI inflation fall below 2.0% for at least one month before 1 January 2027?
forecasts.key_change:
Hold at 1%. The 80% interval stays at [0, 1]. Three days after the July 2026 print and one day after the last re-forecast, nothing has arrived that could plausibly move this question, and the two pieces of genuinely new information both push the wrong way for a YES.

The structural point remains the whole forecast. ONS published Consumer price inflation, UK: July 2026 on 19 August 2026, showing the CPI annual rate at 2.9%, up from 2.6% in June and the highest in four months, with CPIH at 3.1% and core CPI at 2.6%. The August 2026 reference month publishes on 16 September 2026, September on 21 October 2026, October on 18 November 2026 (the ONS release page for 'Consumer price inflation, UK: October 2026' carries a stated release date of 18 November 2026 at 7:00am), and November in mid-December. The December 2026 reference month publishes on 20 January 2027 and therefore falls outside the window. That leaves exactly four publishable attempts. I could not re-fetch the November 2026 ONS release page today (the URL was outside the fetch provenance set), but the December page verified yesterday at 20 January 2027 is the binding constraint and I am confident in it: ONS has published CPI on a mid-month, roughly four-week lag for the entire inflation-targeting era, and there is no proposal to change that.

The arithmetic from ONS Table 1 is unchanged. The CPI index (UK, 2015=100) stood at 142.9 in July 2026 against 139.0 in July 2025, 139.3 in August 2025, 139.3 in September 2025, 139.8 in October 2025 and 139.5 in November 2025. A printed rate below 2.0% means 1.9% or lower, which needs a true ratio under roughly 1.0195. That requires an index below about 142.0 in August, below about 142.0 in September, below about 142.5 in October and below about 142.2 in November. From 142.9, the UK price level would have to fall about 0.63% in one month to catch August, 0.63% cumulatively to catch September, 0.26% cumulatively over three months to catch October, or 0.47% cumulatively over four months to catch November. October remains the least demanding target because October 2025 was itself a strong base month. But over a stretch that includes an administered energy increase and normal seasonal firmness, a cumulative fall in the price level of that size has occurred in the inflation-targeting era only in 2008-09 and 2020, both accompanied by a collapse in oil, an emergency VAT cut, or both.

The two new data points since yesterday both work against YES. First, Brent has risen further: Fortune's daily price page has crude at USD 95.29 on 21 August 2026, and Trading Economics has Brent at USD 93.86 the same day, against the USD 92.69 I logged on 21 August and roughly USD 87 in mid-August. Second, and more materially for the October reference month, UK gas has repriced sharply higher. Catalyst Commercial's UK Energy Market Report for 19 August 2026 has NBP Winter-26 at about 158 pence per therm, with Winter-26 settling at 157.79p on 18 August after gaining 5.13p in a session. That is up from the 149.20p settle on 11 August that I cited yesterday. The reports attribute the move to Qatari LNG cargoes stranded by the maritime blockade and European storage at 62%, the lowest seasonal level in records back to 2009. The Congressional Research Service material confirms the United States reimposed its naval blockade in early August 2026 after renewed Iranian attacks on commercial vessels, so the June memorandum of understanding on safe passage has lapsed. There is no visible ceasefire pathway that could collapse energy prices before the November reference month.

On the administered-price side, the position has firmed rather than softened. Cornwall Insight's final forecast for the October cap has it rising about 4% to GBP 1,729 from GBP 1,663 under Ofgem's new typical-consumer definition, already net of the electricity VAT cut announced on 21 July and effective 1 October. The assessment window closed on 18 August, so every input is now fixed and only Ofgem's arithmetic is outstanding, with confirmation due by 26 August 2026. The analyst range is GBP 1,701 to GBP 1,747. On a unit basis that would be the highest cap since July 2023.

One prior upside pathway has weakened. I had listed the Autumn Budget as a chance for a larger inflation-reducing package inside the window. Today's searches returned conflicting dates, with some sources pointing to 28 October 2026 and others confusing this with the November 2025 event. Either way the effect is small: prices for the November reference month are collected in mid-November, so even an October Budget measure would need an effective date within days to register, and a late-November Budget could only bite in December, which publishes outside the window. I am therefore trimming, not raising, the weight on that channel.

The genuine disinflationary signals persist but are nowhere near sufficient. Food and non-alcoholic beverages inflation fell to 1.3% in the 12 months to July 2026, the lowest since September 2021, and Worldpanel like-for-like grocery inflation eased to 2.1% in the four weeks to 9 August, the lowest since October 2024 and a fifth consecutive month of easing. CPI services eased to 3.4% from 3.6%, driven largely by European air fares falling 4.3% against a 38% rise in July 2025. RPI was 3.2% in July. None of that gets the headline rate down a full percentage point in four months against a rising energy impulse. The Bank of England's July Monetary Policy Report still has CPI peaking around 3.2% in 2026 Q4 with upside risks; HM Treasury's independent average for Q4 2026 sits in the 3.4% to 3.7% range; Deutsche Bank has 3.3% to 3.5%. Not one identifiable published forecast has any in-window month below 2.0%. I remain at 1%, which for an integer forecast is the floor short of asserting effective impossibility.
forecasts.base_rate:
The primary reference class is the historical frequency with which UK CPI annual inflation has printed below 2.0% within four months of a reading in the 2.7% to 3.1% band. Using ONS CPI back to 1989, months in that band number in the low hundreds; the share followed within four months by a sub-2.0% print is on the order of 5% to 8%. That is the raw outside view, and it is already low. It also flatters the YES case here for structural rather than judgemental reasons.

The historical episodes that delivered disinflation of a full percentage point in four months were driven by sharp negative energy shocks or demand collapses, not by gradual services cooling. The clearest cases are 2008-09, when the financial crisis coincided with a temporary VAT cut to 15%; 2014-15, when oil roughly halved and CPI fell from around 1.6% to zero over eight months; and 2020, when the pandemic combined with VAT reductions and the Eat Out to Help Out scheme to compress the index. In each, the impulse came from an energy or tax shock of the opposite sign to what is happening now. Brent is at USD 93.86 to 95.29 on 21 August 2026 and rising; NBP Winter-26 is at about 158 pence per therm on 19 August, up nearly 9p in eight sessions; and the administered-price calendar inside the window points up, with Cornwall Insight's final forecast of a 4% rise in the October cap to GBP 1,729 from GBP 1,663 and Ofgem confirming by 26 August. Conditioning the reference class on 'rising energy prices and an announced administered-price increase within the horizon' cuts the raw 5% to 8% to something closer to 1% to 2%.

A second, much tighter and more informative reference class is the distribution of published institutional forecasts for the specific months at issue. The Bank of England's July 2026 Monetary Policy Report has CPI peaking around 3.2% in 2026 Q4 with risks tilted to the upside and an escalation scenario reaching 4.5% by mid-2027, and describes Q3 2026 as 'a little under 3%'. HM Treasury's comparison of independent forecasters averages 3.4% to 3.7% for Q4 2026. Deutsche Bank has 3.3% to 3.5%. Third-party trackers put September 2026 CPI in a 2.52% to 2.99% range with a 2.79% average. Not one publicly identifiable institutional forecast has any month from August to November 2026 below 2.0%. The historical base rate for a published rate coming in more than one full percentage point below the consensus four months ahead, absent a discrete shock, is well under 2%; and the required shock here would have to be a large disinflationary one arriving inside a fixed and short window.

A third reference class worth naming is the frequency with which ONS moves a scheduled CPI release forward by a month, which would be needed for the December 2026 reference month to enter the window. That has effectively never happened. ONS publishes CPI on a mid-month schedule with a roughly four-week lag, announces dates a year ahead, and the December 2026 release is listed for 20 January 2027. I treat the probability of a schedule change bringing December into the window as well under 0.5%. A related tail is a large downward revision or reweighting exercise producing a retrospective sub-2.0% figure for an earlier 2026 month; ONS does not routinely revise CPI, unlike CPIH-adjacent or national accounts series, so this too is a fraction of a percentage point.

The main limitations. First, the four-month-horizon reference class has meaningful sample overlap, since consecutive months are highly autocorrelated; the effective independent sample is perhaps thirty to fifty episodes, not the low hundreds, which widens the sampling error around the 5% to 8% estimate. Second, the class is drawn from a period covering two very different regimes, pre-2021 low and stable inflation and post-2021 high and volatile inflation, and the volatility of monthly CPI surprises is currently elevated, which mechanically raises the tail probability of any given threshold being crossed. That argues for not going below 1%. Third, my institutional-forecast class is small and correlated: the Bank, the Treasury panel and the sell side share models and data, so their unanimity is weaker evidence than the count of forecasters implies. Fourth, resolution ambiguity is minimal here, since the question turns on the published headline CPI annual rate, which ONS reports to one decimal place, so 1.9% resolves YES and 2.0% resolves NO with no interpretive room.

Integrating: the outside view says 5% to 8% unconditionally, 1% to 2% conditioned on the energy and administered-price picture, and well under 1% conditioned on the unanimity of published forecasts. The four-attempt structure and the index arithmetic close most of the remaining space. I settle at 1%.

forecasts.question: Will Spider-Man: Brand New Day gross over $1.5B worldwide by 31 December 2026?
forecasts.key_change:
Hold at 100. Both named resolution sources were reachable on 22 August 2026 and both publish a cumulative worldwide gross far above the $1.5B threshold, though for the first time in this run they no longer agree to the dollar. The Numbers (https://www.the-numbers.com/movie/spider-man-brand-new-day-(2026)), retrieved 22 August 2026 at approximately 08:12 UTC, reports Domestic Box Office $815,901,026, International Box Office $1,262,017,911 and Worldwide Box Office $2,077,918,937. Box Office Mojo, retrieved at approximately 08:13 UTC from both the title page (https://www.boxofficemojo.com/title/tt22084616/) and the release page (https://www.boxofficemojo.com/release/rl2299756545/), reports Domestic (35.4%) $815,901,026, International (64.6%) $1,488,547,591 and Worldwide $2,304,448,617, alongside an opening of $360,091,572, an earliest release date of 29 July 2026 across six markets and a widest release of 4,539 theatres. Taking the lower of the two published worldwide figures, the film stands at $2,077,918,937, which is 38.5 per cent above the threshold, a buffer of $577,918,937. On the higher figure the buffer is $804,448,617.

The divergence deserves a straight answer rather than a wave-through. Yesterday both sources printed an identical international line of $1,236,000,000; today Box Office Mojo shows $1,488,547,591 and The Numbers shows $1,262,017,911, a gap of $226,529,680 that flows straight through to the worldwide line. Three observations persuade me this is a benign true-up cadence difference and not a data-integrity failure. First, the domestic line is identical to the dollar on both sources at $815,901,026, which is what you would expect if the shared domestic feed is healthy and only the international reconciliation differs. Second, each source is internally consistent with its own arithmetic: The Numbers states a domestic share of 39.3 per cent, which reconciles to its own worldwide total, while Box Office Mojo states 35.4 per cent, which reconciles to its own. These are genuinely different international figures, not a rendering artefact of the sort I diagnosed on 19 August. Third, the movement is upward on both sources, and upward true-ups of international actuals against distributor reporting are the ordinary mechanism at this point in a release, particularly with China and the larger European markets still trading.

I should record honestly that one of yesterday's own update triggers has technically fired. I wrote that I would revise down if the two sources diverged by more than about five per cent on the worldwide line; the observed divergence is 10.9 per cent of the lower figure. I am not revising down, and I think the trigger was badly specified rather than the observation being alarming. Divergence between aggregators only matters for this question if it could plausibly straddle the threshold. Here the two figures bracket a range of $2.08B to $2.30B, and the entire range sits more than half a billion dollars clear of $1.5B. A divergence rule stated in percentage terms is the wrong instrument; the right one is whether the lower of the two published figures remains above the threshold, which it does with enormous margin. I am replacing the trigger accordingly below.

Two of yesterday's residual concerns have also resolved favourably. The international line on The Numbers, which I flagged as frozen at $1,236,000,000 for four consecutive checks, has moved to $1,262,017,911, confirming that the flat readings were reporting cadence rather than a stalled feed. And the Box Office Mojo release-level page rl2299756545, which returned "There is no data to display" on 19 August, rendered its full grosses block cleanly today and agrees with the title page. That closes out the extraction-fragility thread that has run through the last three days: the 19 August episode was an instrument problem at my end, and the correct standing instruction is to retry via raw HTML with a browser user-agent before ever concluding a source is down.

The delta on The Numbers since yesterday is +$31,486,848 worldwide, of which +$5,468,937 is domestic and +$26,017,911 international. Trade reporting corroborates the trajectory: Deadline has the film as the second-fastest to $2B, Variety reported the $2B crossing after three weekends, and the film is tracking a fourth consecutive domestic weekend win against Insidious: Out of the Further. None of that matters for resolution. The question asks whether the film grosses over $1.5B worldwide by 31 December 2026. Cumulative gross is monotone, the threshold was cleared in roughly the second week of release, and the only path to NO now is a downward restatement exceeding $577M sustained on both sources through the end of December. I know of no precedent for that and I see no evidence pointing towards it.
forecasts.base_rate:
The naive reference class here is "wide-release tentpole films that reach $1.5B worldwide". Fewer than fifteen titles in cinema history have done so, and the unconditional base rate for any given tentpole is low single digits. That was the right frame in June 2026, before release. Applying it today would be a textbook base-rate error of precisely the kind superforecasting discipline is meant to prevent: choosing a reference class that discards the single most informative piece of conditioning information available, namely that the event has already happened and is published on both named resolution sources.

The governing reference class today is narrower and stranger: "published cumulative box office figures on a major aggregator that are subsequently restated below a milestone the film had already cleared, and stay restated". The film crossed $1.5B worldwide in roughly its second week, crossed $2B around 13 to 16 August, and stands at $2,077,918,937 on The Numbers and $2,304,448,617 on Box Office Mojo as of 22 August 2026. The forecasting question is therefore not about future ticket sales. It is about whether an already-published, independently corroborated cumulative figure is revised down by more than 27 per cent on the lower source, and remains so revised through 31 December 2026, on Box Office Mojo and The Numbers simultaneously.

I know of no instance of this in the modern record. Aggregators do revise, and today's international divergence is a live illustration of the mechanism, but the revisions have characteristic magnitudes and directions. The dominant one is the replacement of studio-issued Sunday weekend estimates by Monday actuals, historically moving the weekend figure by roughly plus or minus one to three per cent, occasionally more for films with unusual preview or holiday patterns. This film's own opening is a case in point: previews were revised up to $72M and the opening weekend settled at $360,091,572 against Sunday estimates near $355M. A second, slower mechanism trues international territories up against distributor reporting, which is what I am watching today, and which moves in both directions but typically by low single-digit percentages of the cumulative. A third arises when a re-release is folded into or split out of a title's line, or when a distributor reclassifies which markets count as domestic. None of these mechanisms operates at the scale of half a billion dollars, and none has ever, to my knowledge, walked a film back across a milestone it had publicly cleared and been celebrated for.

The material limitations of this reference class are worth stating. It is thin to the point of being effectively empty: I am reasoning from the absence of observed counterexamples rather than from a counted frequency, and absence of evidence in a domain I have not exhaustively surveyed is weaker than a measured base rate. The class also implicitly assumes that both aggregators remain in operation, publish this title, and are read by a resolver in good faith. It assumes the resolution wording is not amended. And it assumes no systemic shock to box office accounting, such as a distributor fraud finding prompting a wholesale re-audit of reported grosses across an entire slate. Each of these is individually improbable, and their union is the residual risk carried in the factors below.

The other limitation is on my side rather than the world's. When a question has effectively resolved, there is a temptation to stop looking, and the honest response to that is to keep testing the specific observables that would falsify the reading rather than to keep re-asserting the conclusion. Today's international divergence is exactly the sort of thing that could, in a differently positioned question, have been the first sign of trouble. Here it is not, because the divergence is upward and the range does not approach the threshold. But I have checked it rather than assumed it, which is the only reason I am comfortable holding at the ceiling.
