forecasts.question: Will OpenAI and Anthropic have a combined ARR exceeding $70B by 31 December 2026?
forecasts.key_change:
Hold at 99. The 21-22 August window delivered a substantial IPO story and two mildly negative demand-side data points, but nothing that touches the arithmetic. The combined run-rate on the dated public record remains roughly $105bn against a $70bn bar, and I can find no path from here to a NO that does not require either a restatement far larger than anyone has alleged or a revenue collapse with no precedent in the sector.

The anchor figures are unchanged. Anthropic: annualised revenue run rate above $65bn as at end-July 2026, reported by Bloomberg on 17 August (bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-17/anthropic-revenue-run-rate-surpasses-65-billion-ahead-of-ipo) and corroborated the same day by TechCrunch, Axios and CNBC, with Fortune following on 18 August. That is up from $47bn in May and roughly $9bn at end-2025, a sevenfold increase in seven months. Anthropic's preliminary Q2 revenue was above $11.5bn (CNBC, 15 August), refined to $11.6bn with a $559m operating profit (WSJ, 18 August), against $4.73bn in Q1 and $787m a year earlier. OpenAI: annualised run rate above $40bn, reported by Bloomberg on 13 August (bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-13/openai-s-revenue-run-rate-tops-40-billion-ahead-of-ipo), roughly $3.3bn a month and roughly double the end-2025 pace. OpenAI's Q2 recognised revenue was $6.7bn, up 18% sequentially from $5.7bn, with operating loss widening to $12.3bn.

What is genuinely new today is the IPO scale reporting. Bloomberg's 21 August newsletter, 'Anthropic Expects to Match or Top SpaceX's Record IPO Size', reports that Anthropic could file publicly as soon as the end of August, debut in October, and target a valuation north of $2 trillion, with the offering sized to match or exceed SpaceX's record $75bn raise ($86.2bn after greenshoe). Fortune ran the same story on 21 August under 'Anthropic to SpaceX: You ain't bigger', and Bloomberg Tech carried it on video the same day. This matters for the question in two ways, both mildly positive. It near-guarantees a public S-1 with audited figures inside the resolution window, which removes most of the residual risk that no credible Q4 figure gets published. And it raises the cost to Anthropic of the headline number proving unsupportable, since a bank syndicate of Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan will have scrubbed the revenue recognition before a $2trn book is opened. That cuts, rather than raises, my estimate of a catastrophic restatement.

The disconfirming evidence I actively went looking for is real but small. Ramp published its August 2026 AI Index on 20 August under the deliberately downbeat title 'Cracks in the AI thesis', and TechCrunch's write-up the same day ('OpenAI is gaining on Anthropic with business users') carries the detail: 43.5% of Ramp's 70,000-plus tracked US businesses paid for Anthropic in July, up 1.1pp month-on-month, against OpenAI at 39.7%, up only 0.23pp, with Ramp economist Ara Kharazian noting OpenAI is growing faster in Q3 to date. Crucially, the share of Ramp businesses paying for any AI rose to nearly 56% in July from just over 50% in March, so the market is still expanding even as the two leaders trade share. Share rotation between OpenAI and Anthropic is neutral for a question about their sum; only aggregate contraction would matter, and the aggregate is growing.

The second negative is pricing. The frontier LLM token price index stood at 12 on 20 August, 88% below its March 2023 base; average enterprise inference costs fell to $1.16-1.18 in the 6-8 August window from $2.04 on 31 May. OpenAI cut GPT-5.6 Luna by 80% on 30 July, and the WSJ reports it is weighing further significant token price reductions to defend share. A third strand: enterprise buyers are reportedly deferring around 25% of planned 2026 AI spend into 2027 amid ROI scrutiny, and H2 enterprise AI spend growth is projected to slow to 6%. Against all this, note that both companies' run rates have doubled or septupled during precisely the period in which token prices fell 88%. Volume growth has overwhelmed unit price declines by an order of magnitude, and there is no sign in the July or August data of that reversing.

The macro backdrop is the weakest part of the bull case, and I hold it as the main reason I am not above 99. The chip complex sold off hard in late July, with Nvidia losing $238bn and the median of 49 AI infrastructure names sitting 40.7% below its all-time high; ECB economists warned on 18 August of a likely valuation correction. But an equity repricing is not a revenue event. Even a severe capital markets dislocation in September would not remove $35bn of annualised contracted and consumption revenue from two firms by December.

The stress tests all clear. On face value figures: $65bn plus $40bn equals $105bn, 50% headroom. On OpenAI's own contention that Anthropic's gross treatment of cloud reseller spend overstates by roughly $8bn: $97bn, 39% headroom. On the harshest defensible reading, trailing-quarter recognised revenue annualised: $11.6bn plus $6.7bn equals $18.3bn, or $73.2bn annualised, which still clears with 4.6% headroom, and Q3 is running above Q2 for both firms on every disclosed indicator (Brockman told staff OpenAI's run rate rose more than 20% month-on-month in July; Friar told investors on 14 August the run rate was up 35% quarter to date with enterprise up 50% QTD and business customer count up 32% in July). Investors quoted by the FT expect Anthropic alone to finish 2026 at a $100bn-$120bn run rate, which would clear the bar without OpenAI contributing anything.

I therefore hold at 99, with the 80% CI at 98-99. The residual 1% is almost entirely resolution mechanics: a resolver adopting an unusually strict net-revenue definition simultaneously with an S-1 haircut materially larger than the $8bn OpenAI alleges. That is a conjunction of two low-probability events, and I see no evidence for either.
forecasts.base_rate:
The governing reference class is not 'will two firms grow into a threshold' but 'a threshold is already exceeded on the public record with roughly 50% headroom four months before the measurement date; will it still be exceeded then'. That is a persistence question, and persistence questions with this structure resolve YES at very high rates. Across public forecasting platforms, questions whose resolution condition is already satisfied by a wide margin, in a domain with a monotonic underlying trend and no identified mechanism for reversal, resolve YES in the high nineties. The correct anchor is 97-99%, and the residual is dominated by resolution mechanics rather than by the world changing.

Three narrower classes point the same way. First, revenue trajectories of large private technology companies at $10bn-plus scale. Documented instances of a firm's disclosed annualised revenue falling more than 30% within two quarters, absent fraud or an exogenous demand collapse, are close to unrepresented. The available cases are Wirecard and FTX, where revenue was substantially fictitious, and the 2020 travel and hospitality shock, where the demand base physically disappeared. Neither template maps onto enterprise AI subscriptions and API consumption in H2 2026, where the observable direction of travel remains budget expansion: Ramp's August 2026 index shows the share of its 70,000-plus business customers paying for AI at all rising from just over 50% in March to nearly 56% in July. The base rate for a 33% two-quarter contraction here is well under 1%.

Second, the reporting-continuity class. Resolution requires credible outlets to publish a Q4 2026 figure for each company. Over the past eighteen months Bloomberg, The Information, the WSJ, CNBC, Reuters and the FT have each published dated run-rate figures for both firms at intervals of six to ten weeks, and the cadence has tightened as both approached public markets. With Anthropic possibly filing a public S-1 by end-August and listing in October, and OpenAI having filed confidentially on 8 June, the volume of audited and semi-audited disclosure over September to December will be higher than at any point in either firm's history. The probability of a Q4 information vacuum is negligible, perhaps 1-2%, and even then a resolver would fall back on the most recent credible figure, which already clears.

Third, the accounting-restatement class for pre-IPO technology companies. Restatements at the S-1 stage do happen, but the distribution of magnitudes is heavily concentrated below 20% of revenue, and gross-versus-net principal-agent reclassifications under ASC 606 are the single most common category. The relevant precedents are Groupon in 2011 (roughly a halving of reported revenue on a gross-to-net reclassification) and, in the other direction, numerous marketplace businesses that survived the change without a demand impact. Groupon is the tail case that keeps me below 99.5%: it demonstrates that a headline can be halved by a definitional change alone. But Anthropic's headline would have to fall by roughly 46% and OpenAI's figure would simultaneously have to be unaffected for the combined sum to breach $70bn, and OpenAI's own hostile estimate of the overstatement is only about $8bn, or 12%.

The principal limitation of this reference-class approach is that all three classes are drawn from eras without a comparable phenomenon. No prior technology cycle produced two private firms growing from $9bn and $20bn to $65bn and $40bn run rates inside eight months. Reference classes built on slower-growing predecessors may understate both upside volatility and downside fragility: a business that can septuple in seven months may in principle be capable of unusual contraction too, because so much of the revenue is consumption-based and switchable rather than contractually locked. I take this seriously, and it is why I do not go above 99. But the asymmetry runs the right way for this question. To resolve NO, the combined figure must fall by a third from where it sits today, and the observable Q3-to-date indicators from both firms point up, not down.

A final limitation: 'ARR' is not a defined accounting term, and the question does not specify a measurement convention. I have stress-tested the three plausible conventions (exit-month annualised, gross versus net, trailing-quarter annualised) and all three clear the bar on current data. That convergence is what justifies a probability in the high nineties rather than the low nineties.

forecasts.question: Will UK average annual real GDP growth exceed 1.5% across the 2030s (2030-2039)?
forecasts.key_change:
Move: 32 to 33. A one-point upward nudge, driven by a single genuinely question-relevant release that yesterday's note did not capture, plus a cluster of smaller cyclical items that all lean the same way.

The material item is the ONS article Blue Book 2026: impact on GDP and main components, published 20 August 2026. This is the annual reconciliation of the national accounts, and for a question that resolves on the ONS-reported arithmetic mean of ten annual growth rates, the systematic direction of ONS revisions is not a second-order detail - it is part of the resolution mechanism. The findings are consistently upward. The level of nominal GDP in 2024 is now 0.5 per cent higher, at 2,905 billion pounds. Cumulative volume growth from 1997 to 2024 is now estimated at 61.7 per cent, revised up from 59.2 per cent, a 2.5 percentage point addition to the level of real GDP accumulated from small annual changes. The mean revision to annual volume growth across 1998 to 2024 was positive 0.06 percentage points. Annual volume growth in 2024 is revised up 0.1 percentage points to 1.1 per cent, and 2023 is also up 0.1 points. Most directly relevant to my reference class, average annual volume growth for 2010 to 2019 is now estimated at 2.1 per cent, revised up 0.1 points, and the 2008-09 peak-to-trough fall is now 6.3 per cent rather than 6.4 per cent, with GDP regaining its pre-downturn level in Q2 2013 rather than Q3 2013. Average annual growth across 1998 to 2024 remains 1.8 per cent to one decimal place, and 1998 to 2007 is unchanged at 2.8 per cent.

Why this moves me at all. The threshold here is 1.5 per cent and my central path for the 2030s sits somewhere around 1.2 to 1.3 per cent, so the question turns on the tail. Anything that adds a persistent, mechanical wedge between true growth and ONS-reported growth compresses that gap. Blue Book 2026 is now the third consecutive vintage in which the direction of travel on real growth revisions has been positive, and the driver is structural rather than random: the incorporation of the Annual Survey of Goods and Services for the majority of service industries for the first time, which contributes positively to the volume growth revision in most years, peaking at 0.17 percentage points in 2010 and 2023. Better measurement of services output is exactly the mechanism I would expect to matter through the 2030s, when the growth that does occur will be disproportionately in hard-to-measure digital and intangible services. If the ONS carries a persistent measurement improvement of roughly plus 0.05 to 0.1 percentage points a year into the 2030s vintages, that is worth a couple of points on a question that hinges on clearing 1.5 rather than 1.4.

I am deliberately not making this larger. The productivity section of the same article is a corrective: output per hour annual growth in 2024 is still estimated as a 0.8 per cent fall, unrevised, and output per worker growth in 2024 is 0.33 per cent, also equal to the previously published estimate. The ONS describes the productivity revisions as minor. So Blue Book 2026 raises the recorded level and the recorded growth of output without improving the picture of the underlying supply side at all - the extra output is being produced by extra hours, not by better productivity. That is a compositional story, and it cannot repeat indefinitely once the labour force stops growing, which on the 2024-based projections it broadly does through the 2030s. The full Blue Book 2026 effects will not be reflected in the productivity statistics until the flash estimate for July to September 2026, publishing 17 November 2026, and the detailed GDP revisions article lands on 30 October 2026 alongside the Blue Book itself, with the quarterly national accounts on 30 September 2026 the first release to incorporate the changes into headline figures. So there is more to learn here.

The remaining items from 21 August are cyclical and roughly consistent with a mild improvement. The S&P Global flash UK composite PMI output index printed 52.5 in August, up from 52.2 in July and above 50 for a second month, on data collected 12 to 19 August, though average cost burdens rose sharply and cost inflation quickened from July's five-month low. GfK consumer confidence rose to minus 14 in August from minus 17, a two-year high. ONS retail sales for July, published 21 August, fell 0.5 per cent on the month, in line with expectations, with core sales down 0.9 per cent against a consensus of minus 0.5 per cent and clothing down 2.7 per cent, but the three-month picture was firmer at plus 1.1 per cent on the previous three months and plus 1.6 per cent on a year earlier - the June promotional pull-forward unwinding rather than a demand break. The HM Treasury comparison of independent forecasts for August 2026 nudged the 2026 consensus to 1.1 per cent from 1.0 per cent in July, and 2027 to 1.2 per cent from 1.1 per cent.

None of that touches the 2030s. Consensus for 2026-27 moving a tenth is noise on a ten-year average that starts four years from now. I record it only because it is directionally the same as the Blue Book news and because it partly offsets the 18 August productivity flash, which was the reason for Thursday's cut from 34 to 32 and which showed RTI-based output per hour up only 0.7 per cent year-on-year in Q2 2026, down from 2.1 per cent in Q1. The structural anchors are unchanged: OBR medium-term TFP growth of 0.8 per cent from the November 2025 outlook rising to 0.8 per cent by 2030, Bank of England potential growth of about 1.3 per cent post-crisis of which 0.8 points was labour supply on Bailey's July 2026 Mansion House framing and staff potential supply growth of only 0.3 to 0.4 per cent currently, and IMF potential of roughly 1.4 per cent. Every official anchor still sits at or below the bar. Next scheduled tests are the QNA on 30 September, the Budget and OBR EFO on 28 October, and the productivity flash on 17 November.
forecasts.base_rate:
The natural reference class is UK decade averages of the annual real GDP growth rate, measured as ONS reports them. Blue Book 2026, published 20 August 2026, has just refreshed these numbers and I now use the revised vintage. Average annual volume growth across 1998 to 2024 is 1.8 per cent. Within that, 1998 to 2007 averaged 2.8 per cent, unchanged in the new vintage. The 2010 to 2019 window now averages 2.1 per cent, revised up 0.1 percentage points. The 1990s on the older ONS basis averaged roughly 2.2 per cent, and the 2000s roughly 1.8 per cent once 2008 and the 4.5 per cent fall in 2009 (itself revised up 0.1 points) are included. The 2020s to date average roughly 1.0 to 1.2 per cent, with 2023 and 2024 now at revised rates and 2024 volume growth at 1.1 per cent.

On that raw count, three of the last four completed decades cleared 1.5 per cent, giving a naive base rate of 60 to 75 per cent with a sample size of four - which is to say, essentially no sample at all. Decade averages are not independent draws. They are four highly serially correlated observations from a single country's history, and the standard error on any inference from them is enormous.

More importantly, the base rate is contaminated in a specific and knowable direction. The pre-2008 decades rested on roughly 2 per cent trend labour productivity growth combined with sustained labour force expansion - rising female participation, later a rising state pension age, and from 2004 EU accession migration. The 2010 to 2019 figure of 2.1 per cent is substantially an output-gap artefact: it measures reflation of an economy that had fallen 6.3 per cent peak to trough and did not regain its pre-downturn level until Q2 2013, not a 2.1 per cent supply-side trend. Productivity growth over that decade was roughly 0.5 per cent a year. Take the output-gap closure out and the 2010s trend was well below the threshold. A forecaster who used the naive four-decade base rate would be extrapolating conditions - two per cent productivity trend, expanding workforce, closing output gap - none of which currently obtain.

The better-matched reference class is the post-2008 UK trend, and better still the post-2019 outturn, because it is a direct read on the exact quantity being forecast. Whole-economy GVA is about 7.1 per cent above its 2019 average as of Q2 2026, roughly 1.0 per cent a year of realised real growth over seven years. On the ONS productivity flash of 18 August 2026, output per hour on the RTI-based measure is 4.6 per cent above the 2019 average, about 0.64 per cent a year, while the LFS-based measure is 2.3 per cent above, about 0.32 per cent a year. Blue Book 2026 confirms output per hour fell 0.8 per cent in 2024 and output per worker rose only 0.33 per cent. Seven years of realised data on this exact question sit a third below the threshold.

A third class worth weighting is the published medium-term projections of institutions that forecast professionally and are scored on it. The OBR cut medium-term TFP growth from 1.1 to 0.8 per cent in November 2025, with potential output growth recovering only to 0.8 per cent TFP by 2030. The Bank of England's post-crisis potential growth estimate is about 1.3 per cent, of which 0.8 points was labour supply that demographics will now withdraw, and staff currently judge potential supply growth at only 0.3 to 0.4 per cent. The IMF's 2026 Article IV put UK potential at about 1.4 per cent. NIESR's trend estimate is about 1.25 per cent. Not one official medium-term anchor sits above 1.5 per cent. If I treat the institutional consensus as roughly 1.1 to 1.4 per cent with a standard deviation of perhaps 0.5 percentage points on a ten-year average, the probability of clearing 1.5 lands in the high twenties to mid thirties.

Limitations worth naming. First, ten-year averages have real dispersion: a single deep recession costs roughly 0.4 to 0.6 points off the decade mean, while a recession before 2030 followed by recovery inside the window would add a similar amount, so the distribution is wide and mildly bimodal. Second, official medium-term forecasts have historically been biased optimistic on productivity, which cuts against me - the OBR has repeatedly had to revise down. Third, ONS revisions have been persistently upward on real growth, and resolution is on ONS-reported figures, which cuts in my favour. Fourth, AI is a genuine structural wildcard with no usable reference class: published estimates of its UK effect span from negligible to over 600 billion pounds of added output by 2035, a range so wide it conveys almost no information. I weight the post-2008 trend class most heavily, the institutional projections second, and the four-decade count least.

factors_up.factor: Blue Book 2026 (ONS, 20 August 2026) confirms a persistent upward revision bias in ONS-reported real growth: mean revision +0.06pp a year across 1998-2024, cumulative 1997-2024 volume growth up from 59.2% to 61.7%, 2024 growth up 0.1pp to 1.1%, 2010-2019 decade average up 0.1pp to 2.1%. Resolution is on ONS-reported figures

AI diffusion is measurably present in the accounts: Bank of England analysis (6 August 2026) shows software and IT consulting contributing 0.1pp to annual productivity growth in 2023-2025, a tenfold rise on the pre-Covid decade, and Q2 2026 GDP detail shows IT consultancy +3.7%, advertising +4.3% and scientific R&D +3.9% q/q

Output-gap mechanics: a soft labour market now (unemployment around 5.0%, payrolled employees falling) raises the odds of a downturn before 2030, which would mechanically lift the 2030s decade average through recovery growth, exactly as the 2010s average of 2.1% was flattered by reflation from a 6.3% peak-to-trough fall

Historical decade base rate: on the revised Blue Book 2026 vintage, 1998-2007 averaged 2.8% and 2010-2019 averaged 2.1%, so a sub-1.5% decade remains unusual by UK long-run standards even if the mechanisms that produced those decades have weakened

Supply-side policy runway before 2030: fiscal devolution to metro mayors from spring 2027, the British Industrial Competitiveness Scheme cutting electricity costs up to 25% for 7,000+ firms from 2027, the Planning and Infrastructure Act's fast-tracking of 150 major infrastructure decisions, and AI Growth Zone data-centre capex

factors_down.factor: Demographics: ONS 2024-based projections put working-age population growth at only about 0.34% a year to 2034, with natural change negative from around 2026 and net migration down to 204,000 in the year to June 2025 from 649,000, leaving trend productivity of 1.1-1.5% a year to do almost all the work
Realised arithmetic on the exact quantity forecast: whole-economy GVA is about 7.1% above its 2019 average as of Q2 2026, roughly 1.0% a year over seven years, a third below the 1.5% threshold

Every official potential-growth anchor sits at or below the bar: OBR medium-term TFP growth cut to 0.8% (November 2025 EFO), Bank of England post-crisis potential 1.3% of which 0.8pp was labour supply and current staff potential supply growth only 0.3-0.4% (April 2026 MPR), IMF potential about 1.4%, NIESR trend about 1.25%

Blue Book 2026's upward GDP revision does not extend to the supply side: output per hour still fell 0.8% in 2024 (unrevised) and output per worker rose just 0.33%, so the extra measured output comes from hours not productivity - a source that cannot repeat once the workforce stops growing

Fiscal drag into the 2030s: July 2026 public sector net borrowing of 1.8bn pounds against an OBR-implied 0.5bn surplus, 56.7bn pounds financial year to date and over 2bn above the OBR path, debt at 94.1% of GDP, with a 30-year gilt around 5.6% and a third successive tax-raising Budget due 28 October 2026

key_uncertainties: Whether AI translates into measured whole-economy total factor productivity in the UK by the early 2030s, or stays concentrated in a narrow ICT and professional-services slice that is 6-8% of GVA. Published estimates of the UK effect span from negligible to over 600bn pounds of added output by 2035 - a range wide enough to convey almost no information

Whether ONS measurement improvements continue to add roughly 0.05-0.1pp a year to reported real growth. Blue Book 2026's ASGS incorporation contributed up to 0.17pp in single years; if that wedge persists into 2030s vintages it materially changes the odds of clearing a 1.5% reported threshold

Whether the UK has a recession before 2030. A downturn inside the late 2020s followed by recovery growth inside 2030-2039 would lift the decade average by perhaps 0.4-0.6pp; a recession inside the window would cut it by a similar amount. The distribution is wide and mildly bimodal on this alone

Whether net migration stabilises near the ONS long-run assumption of about 230,000 a year or stays at the sub-200,000 levels current policy implies. The gap is worth roughly 0.2-0.3pp a year on headline GDP growth through the 2030s
Whether the OBR's 0.8% medium-term TFP assumption is itself too optimistic or too pessimistic. The OBR has repeatedly revised productivity down since 2010, but the November 2025 cut may have overshot
update_triggers: Revise UP if the quarterly national accounts on 30 September 2026 and the GDP revisions in Blue Book 2026 article on 30 October 2026 show a further material upward revision to real growth in recent years, or if the 17 November 2026 productivity flash shows the Blue Book changes lifting output per hour
Revise UP if the ONS productivity flash for Q3 2026 (17 November 2026) shows RTI-based output per hour growth above 1.5% year-on-year, or if two consecutive quarters print above 1.2%

Revise UP if the OBR raises its medium-term trend productivity assumption at the 28 October 2026 Budget EFO, or if the Bank of England revises its potential supply estimate above 0.3-0.4% in the November 2026 Monetary Policy Report

Revise UP if ONS industry-level output-per-hour decomposition shows AI-attributable gains spreading materially outside information and communication into health, construction, retail or public services
Revise UP if a UK recession occurs before 2030 (two consecutive quarters of contraction), raising the odds of recovery-growth arithmetic flattering the 2030s decade average
Revise DOWN if the OBR cuts its trend productivity assumption again at the 28 October 2026 Budget, or if the Budget package is scored as net contractionary for potential output
Revise DOWN if ONS population projections or Home Office data point to net migration settling durably below 150,000 a year, or if working-age population growth to 2034 is revised below 0.3% a year
Revise DOWN if 30-year gilt yields sustain above 6%, forcing further capital spending cuts that reduce public investment through the late 2020s and 2030s
